result:
The proposed answer of 1 is wrong. The solution never derives it and ends with a guess ("it is highly probable that the limit is 1"). An upper bound shows the limit cannot be 1.

**Upper bound.** Let G be K_{2,t+1}-free. Then any two vertices have at most t common neighbors.

Take a copy of K_{t,t} with sides A and B, each of size t. Any pair {u,v} inside A has common neighborhood of size at most t, and it contains B. So the common neighborhood of {u,v} is exactly B. Then every vertex of A is adjacent to all of B, so A lies in the common neighborhood of any pair in B, which has size at most t. Hence A is exactly that common neighborhood.

So each pair of vertices lying on the same side of a K_{t,t} determines that copy uniquely. Each copy uses 2·C(t,2) = t(t−1) such pairs, and distinct copies use disjoint sets of pairs. Therefore the number of copies is at most C(n,2)/(t(t−1)) ≈ n²/(2t(t−1)).

The limit is therefore at most 1/(2t(t−1)), which is less than 1 for t ≥ 3. The answer 1 is impossible. The true value is plausibly 1/(2t(t−1)) if a construction (for example a norm-graph type one at n = t^{2e−1}) tiles almost all pairs, but I have not verified that here. The bound alone is enough to reject the answer.

VERDICT: REJECT
